p.src: Now Cao Cao took advantage of Yuan Shao's defeat, put his troops in order, and pressed steadily on in pursuit. Wearing only a plain headcloth and a single robe, Yuan Shao led some eight hundred horsemen to the northern bank at Liyang, where his general Jiang Yiqu came out from camp to receive him. Yuan Shao related all that had happened, and Jiang Yiqu summoned the scattered troops back to his banner. When the men heard that Yuan Shao was there, they swarmed back around him, and his army recovered its strength. They then resolved to return to Jizhou. On the march, they spent one night in a desolate mountain. From his tent Yuan Shao heard weeping in the distance, so he went secretly to listen. It was a gathering of defeated soldiers, each lamenting the misery of a slain elder brother or a lost younger brother, an abandoned comrade or a dead kinsman, and beating his breast as he wept bitterly. They all said, “Had Lord Tian Feng's counsel been heeded, how could we ever have suffered this calamity?” Yuan Shao bitterly repented, saying, “Because I did not heed Tian Feng's counsel, my army has been defeated and my generals lost. When I return, how can I face him?”

p.src: The next day, while Yuan Shao was riding on, Feng Ji arrived with troops to meet him. Yuan Shao said to Feng Ji, “Because I did not heed Tian Feng's counsel, I have suffered this defeat. Now that I am returning, I am ashamed to face him.” Feng Ji seized the opportunity to slander Tian Feng: “When he heard in prison that my lord's army had been defeated, Tian Feng clapped his hands and laughed, saying, ‘It has turned out exactly as I foresaw!’” Yuan Shao flew into a rage. “How dare that wretched pedant laugh at me! I shall certainly have him killed!” He immediately ordered a messenger to carry a precious sword ahead to the prison in Jizhou and kill Tian Feng.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tian Feng was in prison. One day, a jailer came to him and said, “Congratulations, Assistant Administrator.” Tian Feng asked, “What cause have I for congratulations?” The jailer replied, “General Yuan has returned in crushing defeat. He is certain to value you highly now.” Tian Feng laughed. “Now I shall die!” The jailer asked, “Everyone else rejoices for you. Why do you speak of death?” Tian Feng replied, “General Yuan is outwardly magnanimous but inwardly jealous, and gives no thought to loyal sincerity. Had he won and been joyful, he might still have pardoned me; but now that defeat has brought him shame, I have no hope of living.”

p.src: The jailer did not believe him. Suddenly the messenger arrived bearing the sword and conveyed Yuan Shao's command that Tian Feng's head be taken. Only then was the jailer aghast. Tian Feng said, “I knew all along that I must die.” The jailers all shed tears. Tian Feng said, “For a true man to be born between Heaven and Earth, yet fail to recognize his lord and enter his service, is folly indeed! If I meet death today, what is there to regret?” Thereupon he cut his own throat in the prison. A later poet wrote:

p.src: When Tian Feng was dead, all who heard of it sighed and mourned his loss. Yuan Shao returned to Jizhou, distraught and confused, and paid no attention to affairs of state. His wife, Lady Liu, urged him to appoint an heir. Yuan Shao had three sons. The eldest, Yuan Tan, courtesy name Xianzhong, had been sent to govern Qingzhou; the second, Yuan Xi, courtesy name Xianyi, had been sent to govern Youzhou; the third, Yuan Shang, courtesy name Xianfu, was born to Yuan Shao's later wife, Lady Liu. Handsome and imposing in appearance, he was greatly loved by his father and therefore kept at his side. Ever since the defeat at Guandu, Lady Liu had urged Yuan Shao to make Yuan Shang his heir. Yuan Shao therefore consulted Shen Pei, Feng Ji, Xin Ping, and Guo Tu. As it happened, Shen Pei and Feng Ji had always supported Yuan Shang, while Xin Ping and Guo Tu had always supported Yuan Tan. Each pair served the interests of its own chosen lord.

p.src: Yuan Shao now said to the four, “The threat from without has not yet subsided, but our domestic affairs must also be settled without delay. I intend to discuss the choice of an heir. My eldest son, Tan, is unyielding by nature and fond of killing; my second son, Xi, is weak and timid, and unlikely to accomplish anything; my third son, Shang, bears the aspect of a hero and treats worthy and learned men with courtesy. I wish to appoint him. What do you gentlemen think?” Guo Tu replied, “Of the three sons, Tan is the eldest, and he is presently stationed away from home. If my lord sets aside the elder and appoints the younger, it will sow the seeds of disorder. At present our military prestige has suffered a reverse and enemy troops press upon our borders. How can we permit further strife between father and sons, and among brothers? For now, my lord should attend to the strategy for repelling the enemy. The appointment of an heir may be discussed at a later time.”

p.src: Yuan Shao hesitated and could not decide. Suddenly it was reported that Yuan Xi was coming from Youzhou with sixty thousand troops; that Yuan Tan was coming from Qingzhou with fifty thousand; and that Yuan Shao's nephew Gao Gan was likewise coming from Bingzhou with fifty thousand. All arrived in Jizhou to aid in the war. Yuan Shao rejoiced, reorganized his forces, and went forth to fight Cao Cao. At this time Cao Cao had led his victorious army to deploy along the river, and local people came to welcome him with baskets of food and jars of drink. Seeing several elders whose beards and hair were entirely white, Cao Cao ordered that they be brought into his tent and given seats. He asked them, “How old are you, venerable sirs?” They replied, “We are all nearly a hundred years old.” Cao Cao said, “My soldiers have alarmed and disturbed your countryside, and that weighs heavily upon me.” The elders said, “In the reign of Emperor Huan, a yellow star appeared in the celestial region of Chu and Song. A man of Liaodong named Yin Kui, who was skilled in observing the heavens, once lodged here for the night and told us, ‘A yellow star has appeared in the northwest quarter of the heavens, shining directly upon this place. Fifty years hence, a true sovereign shall arise in the region between Liang and Pei.’ Counting the years to the present, it has been exactly fifty years. Yuan Benchu imposes heavy levies upon the people, and they all resent him. Your Excellency has raised a righteous and benevolent army to relieve the people and punish the guilty. In the single battle of Guandu you broke Yuan Shao's host of a million. This precisely fulfills Yin Kui's words of that time, and the myriad people may now hope for peace.” Cao Cao laughed. “How could I presume to merit what you venerable gentlemen say?” He then presented the elders with wine, food, silk, and cloth, and sent them on their way. He issued an order throughout the army: anyone who entered the countryside and killed a household's chickens or dogs would be punished as though guilty of killing a person. Army and populace alike were awed into submission. Cao Cao too was secretly delighted.

p.src: A report came that Yuan Shao had assembled troops from four provinces, numbering between two and three hundred thousand, and had advanced to Cangting, where he made camp. Cao Cao led his army forward and established his camp. The next day, the two armies faced each other and formed their battle lines. Cao Cao led his officers out before the lines, while Yuan Shao likewise came to the front with his three sons, one nephew, and his civil and military officers. Cao Cao said, “Benchu, your schemes are exhausted and your strength is spent. Why do you still not consider surrender? If you wait until the blade is at your neck, regret will come too late!” Yuan Shao was furious. Looking back at his generals, he cried, “Who dares ride out?” Eager to display his prowess before his father, Yuan Shang flourished his twin swords, spurred his horse from the lines, and galloped back and forth. Cao Cao pointed at him and asked his officers, “Who is that?” Someone who recognized him replied, “That is Yuan Shang, Yuan Shao's third son.”

p.src: Before the words were finished, one of Cao Cao's officers had already ridden forth with leveled spear. Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Shi Huan, an officer under Xu Huang. The two horsemen met, but before three bouts had passed, Yuan Shang wheeled his mount and fled obliquely away. Shi Huan gave chase. Yuan Shang took up his bow, fitted an arrow, twisted around, and shot backward. The arrow struck Shi Huan squarely in the left eye, and he fell from his horse dead. Seeing his son's victory, Yuan Shao pointed forward with his whip, and the massed troops surged into a general melee. After a great slaughter, both sides sounded the gongs, withdrew their troops, and returned to camp. Cao Cao consulted his generals on a strategy to defeat Yuan Shao. Cheng Yu proposed the stratagem of “Ambush on Ten Sides” and advised Cao Cao: “Withdraw your army to the river, conceal ten companies in ambush, and lure Yuan Shao into pursuing you to the bank. With no road of retreat, our men will surely fight to the death, and then we can defeat Yuan Shao.”

p.src: Cao Cao approved the plan. He divided ten companies between the two flanks. On the left, the first was under Xiahou Dun, the second under Zhang Liao, the third under Li Dian, the fourth under Yue Jin, and the fifth under Xiahou Yuan; on the right, the first was under Cao Hong, the second under Zhang He, the third under Xu Huang, the fourth under Yu Jin, and the fifth under Gao Lan. Xu Chu was made vanguard of the central army. The next day, the ten companies advanced first and took their appointed ambush positions on either side. At midnight, Cao Cao ordered Xu Chu to lead troops forward and make a feint of raiding the enemy camp. The troops in all five of Yuan Shao's camps rose at once. Xu Chu turned his force about and fled. Yuan Shao led his army in pursuit amid unceasing battle cries. By daybreak they had pursued Cao Cao's troops to the river, where the Cao army had no road of escape. Cao Cao shouted, “There is no road ahead! Why do you not all fight to the death?” The troops wheeled around and charged forward with all their strength. Xu Chu galloped at their head and slew more than ten enemy officers by his own strength. Yuan Shao's army fell into great disorder. Yuan Shao hurriedly withdrew his army, but Cao Cao's forces came pursuing from behind.

p.src: As they marched on, a drum suddenly sounded: Xiahou Yuan on the left and Gao Lan on the right charged out with their two forces. Yuan Shao gathered his three sons and his nephew around him and fought desperately through a path of blood to escape. Before they had gone another ten li, Yue Jin attacked from the left and Yu Jin from the right, slaughtering Yuan Shao's troops until corpses covered the fields and blood ran in channels. After they had gone scarcely a few more li, Li Dian on the left and Xu Huang on the right led their forces in another intercepting attack. Yuan Shao and his sons, terrified and dismayed, fled into their old camp and ordered the army to prepare a meal. Just as they were about to eat, Zhang Liao from the left and Zhang He from the right came straight at the camp. In panic, Yuan Shao mounted his horse and fled toward Cangting; His men and horses were exhausted and wanted to rest, but Cao Cao's great army came pursuing from behind, and Yuan Shao fled for his life.

p.src: While they were still on the road, Cao Hong from the left and Xiahou Dun from the right blocked their way. Yuan Shao cried, "Unless we fight to the death, we shall surely be captured!" They charged with all their strength and broke free of the encirclement. Yuan Xi and Gao Gan were both wounded by arrows. Almost all their soldiers and horses perished. Yuan Shao embraced his three sons and wept bitterly, then suddenly fainted. Everyone hastened to revive him. Yuan Shao kept vomiting fresh blood and sighed, "I have fought scores of battles, yet never imagined that today I would be reduced to such misery! Heaven itself means to destroy me! Each of you return to your own province and swear to settle once and for all who shall prevail over that villain Cao!" He then ordered Xin Ping and Guo Tu to hurry with Yuan Tan to Qingzhou and restore order there, lest Cao Cao invade its borders; he ordered Yuan Xi to return to Youzhou and Gao Gan to Bingzhou, each to gather and organize troops for future deployment. Yuan Shao took Yuan Shang and the others into Jizhou to recover from his illness, ordering Yuan Shang, Shen Pei, and Feng Ji to take temporary charge of military affairs.

p.src: Now Cao Cao, after his great victory at Cangting, richly rewarded the whole army and sent men to discover the true state of affairs in Jizhou. The spies returned and reported, "Yuan Shao lies ill in bed. Yuan Shang and Shen Pei are keeping strict guard over the city. Yuan Tan, Yuan Xi, and Gao Gan have all returned to their own provinces." Everyone urged Cao Cao to attack at once. Cao Cao said, "Jizhou has vast stores of grain, and Shen Pei is a resourceful strategist; it cannot be taken in haste. The crops are now standing in the fields, and I fear harming the people's livelihood. It will not be too late to take the province after the autumn harvest." While they were discussing this, a letter suddenly arrived from Xun Yu, reporting, "In Runan, Liu Bei has gained the tens of thousands of followers commanded by Liu Pi and Gong Du. Hearing that the Chancellor had led the army north against Hebei, he ordered Liu Pi to defend Runan and personally led troops to exploit the opening and attack Xuchang. The Chancellor should return swiftly with the army to resist him." Greatly alarmed, Cao Cao left Cao Hong to station troops along the river and make a show of strength. Cao Cao himself led the main army toward Runan to meet Liu Bei.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xuande, together with Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun, and the others, led his army toward a surprise attack on the capital at Xu. As they neared the region of Rangshan, they encountered Cao Cao's troops advancing to attack, so Xuande encamped below the mountain. He divided his army into three: Lord Guan stationed troops at the southeastern corner, Zhang Fei at the southwestern corner, while Xuande and Zhao Yun made camp due south. When Cao Cao's army arrived, Xuande came out amid the clamor of drums and shouts. Cao Cao drew up his battle formation and called on Xuande to parley. Xuande rode out beneath the gate banner. Pointing his whip, Cao Cao reviled him: "I treated you as an honored guest. Why have you betrayed righteousness and forgotten my favor?" Xuande replied, "You bear the name of Chancellor of Han, but in truth you are a traitor to the realm! I am a kinsman of the imperial house of Han, and by the Emperor's secret decree I have come to punish a rebel!" He then recited the Girdle Decree aloud from horseback.

p.src: Cao Cao flew into a rage and ordered Xu Chu to give battle. From behind Xuande, Zhao Yun leveled his spear and rode forth. The two generals fought for thirty bouts without either gaining the advantage. Suddenly, mighty battle cries arose, and from the southeastern corner Lord Guan charged in; from the southwestern corner Zhang Fei led his troops in a charge. All three forces fell upon the enemy at once. Cao Cao's troops, wearied by their long march, could not withstand them and fled in a crushing defeat. Victorious, Xuande returned to camp.

p.src: The next day, he again sent Zhao Yun to challenge the enemy. For ten days Cao Cao's troops did not come out. Xuande next sent Zhang Fei to challenge them, but Cao Cao's troops still did not emerge. Xuande grew increasingly suspicious. Suddenly word came that Gong Du, bringing provisions, had been surrounded by Cao Cao's troops, and Xuande hastily ordered Zhang Fei to rescue him. Another report suddenly arrived that Xiahou Dun had led troops around their rear and was advancing directly on Runan. Greatly alarmed, Xuande said, "If this is so, I shall be attacked from front and rear, with nowhere to retreat!" He swiftly dispatched Lord Guan to its rescue. Thus both forces departed.

Xuande next sent Zhang Fei to challenge them, but Cao Cao's troops still did not emerge.

Suddenly word came that Gong Du, bringing provisions, had been surrounded by Cao Cao's troops, and Xuande hastily ordered Zhang Fei to rescue him.

Another report suddenly arrived that Xiahou Dun had led troops around their rear and was advancing directly on Runan. Greatly alarmed, Xuande said, "If this is so, I shall be attacked from front and rear, with nowhere to retreat!"
He swiftly dispatched Lord Guan to its rescue.
Thus both forces departed.

p.src: Within a day, a mounted messenger came to report that Xiahou Dun had already taken Runan, that Liu Pi had abandoned the city and fled, and that Lord Guan was now surrounded. Xuande was greatly alarmed. Then came another report that Zhang Fei, who had gone to rescue Gong Du, had also been surrounded. Xuande urgently wished to withdraw, yet feared Cao Cao's troops would attack from behind. Suddenly it was reported that Xu Chu was outside the camp challenging him, but Xuande dared not ride out. He waited until dawn, ordered his soldiers to eat their fill, sent the infantry ahead and the cavalry after them, while false watch signals continued to sound within the camp. Xuande and his men had gone only a few li from camp when, as they rounded an earthen hill, torches flared everywhere and a great cry came from the summit: "Do not let Liu Bei escape! The Chancellor has been waiting here especially for you!" In panic, Xuande searched for a way of escape. Zhao Yun said, "My lord, do not fear. Only follow me." Zhao Yun leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and cut open a path, while Xuande drew his paired swords and followed behind.

p.src: In the midst of the fighting, Xu Chu caught up and engaged Zhao Yun in a fierce battle. Yu Jin and Li Dian also arrived from behind. Seeing the danger, Xuande fled across the wilderness. Hearing the shouts behind him gradually fade, Xuande turned toward a remote path deep in the mountains and escaped alone on horseback. When at last dawn came, a body of troops suddenly charged out from one side. Xuande was greatly alarmed, but looking closely saw Liu Pi approaching with more than a thousand defeated horsemen, escorting Xuande's family; Sun Qian, Jian Yong, and Mi Fang were also there. They explained, "Xiahou Dun's army attacked with tremendous force, so we abandoned the city and fled. Cao Cao's troops pursued us, but fortunately Lord Guan held them back, allowing us to escape." Xuande said, "I wonder where Lord Guan is now?" Liu Pi replied, "General, let us press on for now; we can attend to that afterward."

p.src: After they had gone several li, a roll of drums sounded and a body of troops surged out ahead. The general at their head was Zhang He, who shouted, "Liu Bei, dismount at once and surrender!" Just as Xuande was about to retreat, he saw a red banner wave on the hilltop. An army poured out of the mountain hollow, led by the general Gao Lan. With no road open in either direction, Xuande looked up to heaven and cried, "Why does Heaven bring me to such desperate straits? Since matters have come to this, I would sooner die!" He made to draw his sword and cut his own throat. Liu Pi hastily stopped him, saying, "Allow me to fight to the death, seize a path, and save you, my lord." With that, he rode forward to engage Gao Lan. Before three bouts had passed, Gao Lan cut him down from his horse with a single stroke.

p.src: As Xuande panicked and was about to fight for himself, Gao Lan's rear ranks suddenly fell into disorder. A general charged through the formation, and at the thrust of his spear Gao Lan tumbled from his horse. They looked and saw that it was Zhao Yun. Xuande was overjoyed. Zhao Yun spurred his horse and leveled his spear, scattering the rear ranks, then came against the vanguard and fought Zhang He single-handed. Zhang He fought Zhao Yun for more than thirty bouts, then wheeled his horse and fled in defeat. Zhao Yun pressed the advantage and charged after him, but Zhang He's troops held the mountain pass, and the narrow road left no way through.

p.src: While they were fighting to seize the road, Lord Guan, Guan Ping, and Zhou Cang appeared with three hundred soldiers. Attacking from both sides, they drove Zhang He back. They passed out through the defile, occupied the strategic heights, and made camp. Xuande sent Lord Guan to seek Zhang Fei. It turned out that when Zhang Fei went to rescue Gong Du, Gong Du had already been slain by Xiahou Yuan. Zhang Fei fought fiercely and drove Xiahou Yuan back, then pursued him, only to be surrounded by troops under Yue Jin. Lord Guan encountered routed soldiers on the road, followed their trail, drove Yue Jin back, and returned with Zhang Fei to see Xuande.

p.src: Word came that Cao Cao's main army was pursuing them, so Xuande ordered Sun Qian and the others to escort the families ahead. Xuande remained behind with Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun, fighting as they withdrew. Seeing that Xuande had gone far, Cao Cao recalled his troops and did not pursue. Xuande's defeated army numbered fewer than a thousand and fled in wretched disorder. They came to a river ahead and, upon asking the local people, learned that it was the Han River. Xuande encamped there for the time being. The local people recognized Xuande and presented him with sheep and wine, whereupon everyone gathered to drink on the riverbank. Xuande sighed, saying, “All of you possess the talent to aid a king, yet unhappily you have followed Liu Bei. My fortunes are straitened, and I have brought hardship upon you all. Today I have not even a place to stand, and I truly fear that I shall ruin your prospects. Why do you not leave me and enter the service of an enlightened lord, that you may win achievement and renown?”

p.src: They all covered their faces and wept. Guan Yu said, “Brother, you are mistaken. When Gaozu contended with Xiang Yu for the empire, he was defeated by Yu many times; but afterward he prevailed in a single battle at Jiuli Mountain and founded a dynasty that endured four hundred years. Victory and defeat are the common lot of soldiers; how can you cast down your own resolve?” Sun Qian said, “Success and failure each have their appointed time; you must not lose heart. Jingzhou is not far from here. Liu Jingsheng holds sway over the Nine Provinces, with strong troops and ample provisions; moreover, he and you are both kinsmen of the imperial house of Han. Why not seek refuge with him?” Xuande said, “I fear only that he will not receive me.” Sun Qian said, “I am willing to go ahead and persuade him, so that Jingsheng will come beyond his borders to welcome you, my lord.”

p.src: Xuande was overjoyed and immediately sent Sun Qian traveling through the night to Jingzhou. Upon reaching the commandery, Sun Qian entered and was received by Liu Biao. After the formal greetings, Liu Biao asked, “You serve Xuande; why have you come here?” Sun Qian replied, “Imperial Inspector Liu is a hero of the realm. Though his troops and generals are few, his ambition is to uphold the dynasty. Liu Pi and Gong Du of Runan had no former ties of kinship or friendship with him, yet they too repaid him with their lives. You, illustrious lord, and the Imperial Inspector are both descendants of the imperial house of Han. Now, newly defeated, the Imperial Inspector intended to go east of the Yangzi and seek refuge with Sun Zhongmou. I remonstrated with him, saying, ‘You must not turn your back on kin and seek out strangers. General Liu of Jingzhou honors the worthy and humbles himself before scholars; men of talent flock to him as water flows eastward. How much more warmly, then, would he receive one of his own clan?’ Therefore the Imperial Inspector has specially sent me ahead to make this appeal and await your command, illustrious lord.”

p.src: Liu Biao was delighted and said, “Xuande is my younger brother. I have long wished to meet him, but never had the opportunity. If he is willing to favor me with a visit now, I shall be truly fortunate.” Cai Mao slanderously objected, “You must not receive him. Liu Bei first followed Lü Bu, then served Cao Cao, and lately sought refuge with Yuan Shao, yet in every case he failed to remain to the end. This is enough to show what manner of man he is. If you receive him now, Cao Cao will surely send troops against us, needlessly embroiling us in war. It would be better to behead Sun Qian and present his head to Cao Cao; Cao Cao would then surely treat you with great favor, my lord.” Sun Qian answered sternly, “I am not a man who fears death. Imperial Inspector Liu is loyal at heart and devoted to the state; he cannot be compared with Cao Cao, Yuan Shao, Lü Bu, and their kind. His former associations with them arose only from necessity. Now, hearing that General Liu is descended from the Han and bound to him by the close ties of common ancestry, he has come a thousand li to seek refuge. Why do you offer such slanders and show such jealousy of the worthy?”

p.src: On hearing this, Liu Biao rebuked Cai Mao: “My decision is made. Say no more.” Cai Mao withdrew, ashamed and resentful. Liu Biao then ordered Sun Qian to go ahead and inform Xuande, while he himself traveled thirty li beyond the city walls to welcome him. When Xuande met Liu Biao, he observed the rites with the utmost deference. Liu Biao likewise treated him with great generosity. Xuande presented Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and the others to Liu Biao; then Liu Biao entered Jingzhou together with Xuande and assigned houses for them to inhabit.

p.src: Now Cao Cao's scouts learned that Xuande had gone to Jingzhou and sought refuge with Liu Biao, whereupon Cao Cao wished to lead an army against him. Cheng Yu said, “Yuan Shao has not yet been eliminated. If we hastily attack Jingzhou and Xiangyang and Yuan Shao rises in the north, the outcome will be impossible to foretell. It would be better to withdraw to the capital at Xu, rest the army, and build up its strength. When warm weather returns next spring, we can first lead our troops to destroy Yuan Shao and afterward seize Jingzhou and Xiangyang. Thus the advantages of both north and south may be secured in a single campaign.”

p.src: Cao Cao approved his counsel and accordingly led the army back to the capital at Xu. In the first month of spring in the eighth year of Jian'an, Cao Cao again deliberated on raising an army. He first dispatched Xiahou Dun and Man Chong to hold Runan against Liu Biao. He left Cao Ren and Xun Yu to guard the capital at Xu. He personally commanded the main army, advanced to Guandu, and encamped there.
